results.topic: Blender 5.2.1 LTS headless feasibility: glTF exporter, Cycles/Metal lightmap bakes + denoise, UV2 atlases, modeling, characters (skin/auto-weights/cloth/shape keys), 5.x layered Action API + NLA, materials/color management, bundled fonts/assets, bake timing (M1 7-core GPU, 8 GB)

findings.question: Which Blender build did the experiments use, and how were they run?
findings.answer: Blender 5.2.1 LTS (hash 9e2066aef7ef, built 2026-08-25). Every run used /Applications/Blender.app/Contents/MacOS/Blender --background --factory-startup [--log cycles --log-level info] --python-expr "$(cat <<'PY' ... PY)". Everything stayed in memory: images were created with bpy.data.images.new, no save/export operator was called, and no output path was set. Each run took 1.7 to 13.6 s wall. Cycles Metal kernels were already cached in ~/.cache/cycles/kernels/Apple_M1, so there was no kernel-compile stall.

findings.question: What is the full property list of bpy.ops.export_scene.gltf, with enum items (format, image format, animation mode, Draco/meshopt, texcoords/normals/tangents/color attributes, morph, skins, NLA, sampling, merge, lights, cameras, extras, apply, selection/collection)?
findings.answer:
The exporter (io_scene_gltf2 version 5.2.40) has 110 RNA properties; the full list with types and defaults is in exact_snippets.
- export_format: items come from the callback get_format_items. 'GLB' is the default (index 0), then 'GLTF_SEPARATE'. 'GLTF_EMBEDDED' appears only if the addon preference allow_embedded_format is set.
- export_image_format: AUTO, JPEG, WEBP, NONE (default AUTO).
- export_animation_mode: ACTIONS, ACTIVE_ACTIONS, BROADCAST, NLA_TRACKS, SCENE (default ACTIONS).
- export_merge_animation: NLA_TRACK, ACTION, NONE (default ACTION).
- export_vertex_color: MATERIAL, ACTIVE, NAME, NONE (default MATERIAL), plus export_all_vertex_colors=True and export_active_vertex_color_when_no_material=True. There is no export_colors property.
- Draco: export_draco_mesh_compression_enable=False, level 6, quantization position 14, normal 10, texcoord 12, color 10, generic 12.
- Meshopt: export_meshopt_compression_enable=False; export_meshopt_extension is EXT_meshopt_compression (default) or KHR_meshopt_compression. libbf_intern_draco_bridge.dylib and libbf_intern_meshopt_bridge.dylib ship in the addon folder.
- Other defaults: export_texcoords=True, export_normals=True, export_tangents=False, export_skins=True, export_influence_nb=4, export_all_influences=False, export_morph=True, export_morph_normal=True, export_morph_tangent=False, export_morph_animation=True, export_morph_reset_sk_data=True, export_try_sparse_sk=True, export_try_omit_sparse_sk=False, export_nla_strips=True, export_force_sampling=True, export_frame_step=1, export_optimize_animation_size=True, export_bake_animation=False, export_anim_single_armature=True, export_lights=False, export_cameras=False, export_extras=False, export_apply=False, export_yup=True, use_selection=False, use_visible=False, use_renderable=False, use_active_collection=False, use_active_collection_with_nested=True, use_active_scene=False, collection=''.

findings.question: Do multiple UV maps export as TEXCOORD_0 / TEXCOORD_1?
findings.answer: Yes, according to the source. In primitive_extract.py, prepare_data() sets tex_coord_max = len(self.blender_mesh.uv_layers) whenever gltf_texcoords is on. The attribute loop then emits every layer i as 'TEXCOORD_' + str(i) in mesh.uv_layers order, and does not filter by material usage. V is flipped to (u, 1-v) in __get_uvs_attribute. A mesh with layers [UVMap, Lightmap] therefore gets UVMap as TEXCOORD_0 and Lightmap as TEXCOORD_1. This is verified from source only; no export was run, per the rules.

findings.question: What are the exact parameters of bpy.ops.object.bake?
findings.answer:
There are 22 parameters:
- type: COMBINED (default), AO, SHADOW, POSITION, NORMAL, UV, ROUGHNESS, EMIT, ENVIRONMENT, DIFFUSE, GLOSSY, TRANSMISSION
- pass_filter (enum flag set): NONE, EMIT, DIRECT, INDIRECT, COLOR, DIFFUSE, GLOSSY, TRANSMISSION; default empty
- filepath, width=512, height=512, margin=16
- margin_type: ADJACENT_FACES or EXTEND (the operator defaults to EXTEND; scene BakeSettings defaults to ADJACENT_FACES)
- use_selected_to_active, max_ray_distance, cage_extrusion, cage_object
- normal_space: OBJECT or TANGENT; normal_r / normal_g / normal_b
- target: IMAGE_TEXTURES or VERTEX_COLORS
- save_mode: INTERNAL (default) or EXTERNAL
- use_clear (operator default False; BakeSettings default True), use_cage, use_split_materials, use_automatic_name, uv_layer (string)
Relevant Cycles settings: scene.cycles.samples defaults to 4096 and use_adaptive_sampling defaults to True, so set both explicitly. max_bounces is 12, diffuse_bounces 4, use_light_tree True.

findings.question: Does a tiny Metal bake work (32x32, type DIFFUSE, pass_filter {'DIRECT','INDIRECT'}, 8 samples), and how long does it take?
findings.answer:
Yes. The bake returned {'FINISHED'} with the message 'Info: Baking map saved to internal image...', so the result stays in memory.
- The first call took 0.787 s, which includes loading Metal kernels and pipelines.
- The second call took 0.279 s.
- The same bake with device='CPU' took 0.011 s and gave the same statistics (mean 0.9227, max 2.0861).
The Cycles log shows 'Path tracing on: Apple M1 (GPU - 7 cores) (Metal) ... Hardware Ray-Tracing: Off', and cp.has_active_device() returned True. Each Metal bake session pays about 0.09 to 0.16 s for its first sample, so for tiny bakes the CPU is faster.

findings.question: Is denoising applied to bakes in 5.2 (scene.cycles.use_denoising)?
findings.answer: No. scene.cycles.use_denoising defaults to True, and the denoiser enum offers only 'OPENIMAGEDENOISE', but it has no effect on bakes. A 64x64 bake at 4 spp (same seed, adaptive sampling off) with use_denoising=True differs from the use_denoising=False bake by at most 3.6e-7. That is the same jitter seen between two identical non-denoised bakes, which are not bit-exact on the GPU. RMSE against a 64 spp reference was 0.08305 in both cases. Bakes must be denoised afterwards.

findings.question: How can bakes be denoised afterwards, in memory and headless?
findings.answer:
Use Blender's bundled OIDN through ctypes. OIDN 2.5.0 ships inside the app (oidnGetDeviceInt(dev, 'version') returns 20500) as /Applications/Blender.app/Contents/Resources/lib/libOpenImageDenoise.dylib, alongside _core, _device_cpu and _device_metal.
- It can be called from Blender's Python with numpy buffers taken from img.pixels (code in exact_snippets).
- The 'RT' filter with hdr=True works: RMSE on a 64x64 4 spp bake dropped from 0.0831 to 0.0320. A 1024x1024 image takes 0.508 s on the CPU device.
- 'RTLightmap' exists but oidnCommitFilter fails with 'unsupported combination of input features' (its weights were not built in), so it is unavailable.
- The Metal OIDN device (type 5) can be created but was never run.
The compositor route did not work as tested:
- CompositorNodeDenoise exists, with inputs Image, Albedo, Normal, HDR (bool socket), Prefilter and Quality (menu sockets).
- Scene.compositing_node_group exists; Scene.node_tree no longer exists.
- A headless bpy.ops.render.render(write_still=False) with Image → Denoise → Viewer (plus a Group Output) returned FINISHED in 0.17 s, but the 'Viewer Node' image stayed 256x256 and all zeros.

findings.question: How do you create a UV2 for lightmaps and bake into it?
findings.answer:
Create it with mesh.uv_layers.new(name='Lightmap') (signature: new(name, do_init)).
- Unwrap and pack operators act on uv_layers.active, so set that first. active_render stays on 'UVMap'.
- bpy.ops.object.bake(..., uv_layer='Lightmap') bakes through UV2 even when UVMap is both active and active_render.
- Test: with UV2 squeezed into the left half of the image, 100% of left-half texels were baked (mean 1.12) and 0% of right-half texels.

findings.question: What are the parameters of uv.lightmap_pack, uv.smart_project and uv.pack_islands in 5.2, and does multi-object packing into one atlas work?
findings.answer:
Parameters:
- lightmap_pack: PREF_CONTEXT (SEL_FACES default, or ALL_FACES), PREF_PACK_IN_ONE=True, PREF_NEW_UVLAYER=False, PREF_BOX_DIV=12, PREF_MARGIN_DIV=0.1.
- smart_project: angle_limit=1.1519 rad, margin_method (SCALED default, ADD, FRACTION), rotate_method (AXIS_ALIGNED, AXIS_ALIGNED_X, AXIS_ALIGNED_Y default), island_margin=0, area_weight=0, correct_aspect=True, scale_to_bounds=False.
- pack_islands: udim_source (CLOSEST_UDIM default, ACTIVE_UDIM, ORIGINAL_AABB, CUSTOM_REGION), rotate=True, rotate_method (ANY default, CARDINAL, AXIS_ALIGNED, AXIS_ALIGNED_X, AXIS_ALIGNED_Y), scale=True, merge_overlap=False, margin_method (SCALED default, ADD, FRACTION), margin=0.001, pin=False, pin_method (SCALE, ROTATION, ROTATION_SCALE, LOCKED default), shape_method (CONCAVE default, CONVEX, AABB).
- uv.average_islands_scale: scale_uv, shear.
Multi-object packing works both ways (tested on 3 objects: cube, UV sphere, cylinder):
- lightmap_pack in object mode on all selected objects, with ALL_FACES and PACK_IN_ONE: 0 overlap pixels, 86.6% coverage, UVs within [0.002, 0.998], and the original UVMap untouched.
- Multi-object edit mode (context.objects_in_mode held all 3) with use_uv_select_sync=True, then select_all, smart_project, average_islands_scale and pack_islands: 0 cross-object and 0 self-overlap pixels, 59.1% coverage, UVs within [0.005, 0.995].

findings.question: What modeling features does 5.2 offer: Boolean solvers, curve bevel profiles, core modifiers, bmesh?
findings.answer:
- Boolean modifier solver items are FLOAT, EXACT and MANIFOLD ('FAST' is now 'FLOAT'). All three evaluated a cube minus sphere, giving 28, 32 and 31 vertices. operand_type is OBJECT or COLLECTION.
- Curve bevel_mode items are ROUND, OBJECT and PROFILE.
- CurveProfile.preset items are LINE, SUPPORTS, CORNICE, CROWN and STEPS. There is no CUSTOM item; assigning 'CUSTOM' raises TypeError.
- A custom profile is built with curve.bevel_profile.points.add(x, y) followed by profile.update(). It only changes the evaluated geometry after curve.update_tag() (max |y,z| went from 0.200 to 0.206). CurveProfile functions are update, reset_view, initialize and evaluate.
- SOLIDIFY, BEVEL, ARRAY, SUBSURF, WELD, SHRINKWRAP, DATA_TRANSFER (loop CUSTOM_NORMAL), TRIANGULATE, DISPLACE and DECIMATE were all added with obj.modifiers.new and evaluated via depsgraph to_mesh(). Other available types include SKIN, NODES, MIRROR, SCREW, REMESH, WIREFRAME, CLOTH and ARMATURE.
- bmesh works (bmesh.ops.create_cube, create_uvsphere and create_grid, then to_mesh).
- Material.use_nodes is deprecated ('expected to be removed in Blender 6.0'); new materials already contain Principled BSDF and Material Output nodes.

findings.question: Does a Skin modifier skeleton plus object.skin_armature_create work in background via temp_override, creating an armature and vertex groups? How many bones?
findings.answer:
Yes. Test setup: a 5-vertex, 4-edge skeleton with obj.modifiers.new('Skin','SKIN'), which auto-creates me.skin_vertices[0]; every vertex got radius=(0.15,0.15) and use_root was set on vertex 0. The evaluated skin mesh has 52 vertices and 52 faces.
Calling skin_armature_create(modifier='Skin') inside temp_override(object, active_object, selected_objects, selected_editable_objects), with no view-layer active object, returned FINISHED. It created an object 'Armature' with 4 bones (Bone.00 to Bone.03, one per edge). The mesh gained vertex groups Bone.00 to Bone.03 and the modifier stack became [Skin, Armature]; the mesh was not parented.

findings.question: Does parent_set(type='ARMATURE_AUTO') work in background on a simple mesh plus a 2-bone armature?
findings.answer:
Yes, using real view-layer selection: mesh and armature selected, armature active.
- Test mesh: a 242-vertex capsule (UV sphere scaled z×3.3, scale applied); bones 'Lower' (0 to 1) and 'Upper' (1 to 2, connected).
- Result {'FINISHED'}: 161 vertices have weight > 0.01 in 'Lower' and 161 in 'Upper', so bone heat produced non-empty groups.
- An ARMATURE modifier targeting the rig was added and the mesh was parented to the rig.

findings.question: Does a Cloth modifier simulate when stepping scene.frame_set(1..5) in background?
findings.answer: Yes. On a 10x10 grid with the Cloth modifier at defaults (quality 5, cache frames 1 to 250), mean local z at frames 2 to 5 was -0.0058, -0.0210, -0.0454 and -0.0785. Maximum vertex displacement from frame 1 to frame 5 was 0.0785. The cache stayed in memory (point_cache.is_baked False).

findings.question: Do shape keys work, and which glTF export options carry them?
findings.answer:
Shape keys work: ob.shape_key_add(name='Basis') then ob.shape_key_add(name='Open', from_mix=False), with key.data[i].co edited. At value 0.5 the evaluated vertex mixes correctly (z = -0.5). key.keyframe_insert('value') creates an action on the Key datablock. glTF options that carry them (verified from RNA and source, not by an export run):
- export_morph=True
- export_morph_normal=True
- export_morph_tangent=False
- export_morph_animation=True
- export_morph_reset_sk_data=True
- export_try_sparse_sk=True
- export_try_omit_sparse_sk=False
export_apply's own description reads 'Apply modifiers (excluding Armatures) to mesh objects - WARNING: prevents exporting shape keys'.

findings.question: How does the 5.x Action API work (slots, layers, strips, channelbags, fcurves.new)? Does legacy action.fcurves exist? Does pose_bone.keyframe_insert work?
findings.answer:
Legacy access is gone: action.fcurves raises AttributeError ('Action' object has no attribute 'fcurves'), and the Action RNA has no fcurves, groups or id_root. It does have slots, layers, is_action_legacy and is_action_layered.
Verified signatures:
- ActionSlots.new(id_type*, name*)
- ActionLayers.new(name*)
- ActionStrips.new(type='KEYFRAME')
- ActionKeyframeStrip.channelbag(slot*, ensure=False)
- ActionChannelbagFCurves.new(data_path*, index=0, group_name='')
- NlaTracks.new(prev=None)
- NlaStrips.new(name*, start*, action*)
The working code is in exact_snippets; the Tip bone quaternion at frame 21 evaluated to (0.924, 0.383, 0, 0) and the slot identifier is 'OBRig'. bpy_extras.anim_utils provides action_ensure_channelbag_for_slot, action_get_channelbag_for_slot, action_get_first_suitable_slot and animdata_get_channelbag_for_assigned_slot. pose_bone.keyframe_insert('rotation_quaternion', frame=1) returns True and auto-creates action 'RigAction' with slot 'OBRig' (1 layer, 1 strip).

findings.question: Does bpy.ops.nla.bake (visual keying of an IK-constrained bone) work in background?
findings.answer:
Yes. Setup: a 2-bone chain with an IK constraint (chain_count 2) targeting an empty keyed at frames 1 and 10. In POSE mode with pose.select_all(action='SELECT') (context.selected_pose_bones returned both bones), nla.bake(frame_start=1, frame_end=10, only_selected=True, visual_keying=True, clear_constraints=True, bake_types={'POSE'}, channel_types={'LOCATION','ROTATION','SCALE'}) returned {'FINISHED'}.
- It created a new action 'Action' with slot OBRig: 20 fcurves (2 bones × 10 channels), 10 keys each.
- The IK constraint was removed.
- The baked Root rotation at frame 1 is [0.931, -0.273, 0.139, -0.199] and at frame 10 is [0.931, -0.273, -0.139, 0.199], so the IK motion was captured.

findings.question: How do you put several actions on NLA tracks so the glTF exporter emits them as separate animations, and with which export_animation_mode?
findings.answer:
Runtime part (verified): tr = ob.animation_data.nla_tracks.new(); tr.name = 'Walk'; st = tr.strips.new('Walk', 1, action). strip.action_slot is auto-assigned ('OBRig') when the action has one OBJECT slot.
Exporter part (read from source, not export-tested): with export_animation_mode='ACTIONS' (the default), action.py collects:
- the active action, if animation_data.action_slot is set;
- the strip of every NLA track with exactly one non-muted strip whose action_slot is not None, each as its own glTF animation.
It skips, with warnings, tracks holding more than one non-muted strip and strips without an action_slot. Also:
- export_anim_single_armature=True (default) adds every action in bpy.data.actions that has an OBJECT slot animating bones, when the export contains exactly one armature and it has animation_data.
- NLA_TRACKS mode exports one animation per track.
- export_merge_animation='ACTION' (default) merges animations of different objects by action name.
- The exporter reads only the first layer and first strip of each action (get_channelbag_for_slot).

findings.question: Materials: which bpy.types names start with ShaderNodeTex, what are the noise enums, and what are the Principled BSDF inputs in 5.2?
findings.answer:
ShaderNodeTex* types: ShaderNodeTexBrick, Checker, Coord, Environment, Gabor, Gradient, IES, Image, Magic, Noise, Sky, Voronoi, Wave, WhiteNoise.
- ShaderNodeTexNoise.noise_type: MULTIFRACTAL (default), RIDGED_MULTIFRACTAL, HYBRID_MULTIFRACTAL, FBM, HETERO_TERRAIN.
- noise_dimensions: 1D, 2D, 3D, 4D (4D is available; the RNA default is '1D').
- Voronoi: dimensions 1D to 4D; feature F1, F2, SMOOTH_F1, DISTANCE_TO_EDGE, N_SPHERE_RADIUS; distance EUCLIDEAN, MANHATTAN, CHEBYCHEV, MINKOWSKI.
- Gabor: gabor_type 2D or 3D.
- Sky: SINGLE_SCATTERING, MULTIPLE_SCATTERING, PREETHAM, HOSEK_WILKIE.
- WhiteNoise: 1D to 4D.
Principled BSDF inputs, in order: Base Color, Metallic, Roughness, IOR, Alpha, Thin Wall (BOOLEAN, new), Normal, Weight, Diffuse Roughness, Subsurface Weight, Subsurface Radius, Subsurface Scale, Subsurface IOR, Subsurface Anisotropy, Specular IOR Level, Specular Tint, Anisotropic, Anisotropic Rotation, Tangent, Transmission Weight, Coat Weight, Coat Roughness, Coat IOR, Coat Tint, Coat Normal, Sheen Weight, Sheen Roughness, Sheen Tint, Emission Color, Emission Strength, Thin Film Thickness, Thin Film IOR. Enums: distribution GGX or MULTI_GGX; subsurface_method BURLEY, RANDOM_WALK, RANDOM_WALK_SKIN, RANDOM_WALK_LEGACY.

findings.question: Which ImageFormatSettings.file_format items and color-management names are available?
findings.answer:
File formats with media_type IMAGE: AVIF, JPEG, OPEN_EXR, PNG, WEBP, BMP, CINEON, DPX, IRIS, JPEG2000, HDR, TARGA, TARGA_RAW, TIFF. OPEN_EXR_MULTILAYER and FFMPEG appear under media_type MULTI_LAYER_IMAGE and VIDEO.
- color_depth: 8, 10, 12, 16, 32.
- exr_codec: NONE, ZIP, PIZ, DWAA, DWAB, HTJ2K, ZIPS, RLE, PXR24, B44, B44A.
- A new float image defaults to colorspace 'Linear Rec.709'.
The full colorspace list is in exact_snippets; it includes 'sRGB', 'Linear Rec.709', 'Non-Color', 'ACEScg', 'AgX Base sRGB', 'Khronos PBR Neutral sRGB', 'Display P3' and 'scene_linear'.
- View transforms: Standard, ACES 1.3, ACES 2.0, Khronos PBR Neutral, AgX, Filmic, Filmic Log, False Color, Raw.
- Displays: sRGB, Display P3, Rec.1886, Rec.2020, Rec.2100-PQ, Rec.2100-HLG.
- Looks: None, plus AgX Punchy, Greyscale and seven contrast levels.
Saving any of these formats to disk was not exercised.

findings.question: Which font files ship with Blender, and under what licenses?
findings.answer:
bpy.utils.system_resource('DATAFILES', path='fonts') is /Applications/Blender.app/Contents/Resources/5.2/datafiles/fonts. It contains only .woff2 files:
- Inter.woff2 (351 KB)
- DejaVuSansMono.woff2 (145 KB)
- Noto Sans CJK Regular.woff2 (11.4 MB)
- NotoEmoji-VariableFont_wght.woff2
- about 20 NotoSans* script fonts (Arabic, Devanagari, Math, Symbols, and so on)
Licenses, per /Applications/Blender.app/Contents/Resources/text/license/license.md: Inter is SIL OFL 1.1 ('Copyright 2020 The Inter Project Authors'); Noto is OFL 1.1; DejaVu Sans Mono is Bitstream Vera + Arev ('DejaVu changes are in public domain'). The OFL text is in text/license/spdx/OFL-1.1.txt.
bpy.data.fonts.load works on the woff2 files: Inter loads as 'Inter Variable Regular' (text 'Exit' gives 336 vertices / 360 faces) and DejaVu as 'DejaVu Sans Mono Book'.

findings.question: Timing: how long does a closed room (6 inward planes + point light) lightmap take at 128x128 / 64 spp on Metal?
findings.answer:
1.974 s wall (Cycles log confirms Metal), with the 6 planes as separate objects in one bake call. Each selected object gets its own Cycles session, so the log shows 6 'Path tracing on ... (Metal)' blocks. Each session costs about 0.26 s wall, of which the first sample is about 0.09 to 0.12 s; the 63 remaining samples take about 0.073 s per object.
The same room as one joined mesh at 64x64 took 0.28 to 0.45 s regardless of spp (1, 16, 64), and 0.80 s at 256 spp. The CPU session overhead is only about 0.027 s per object: 6 separate objects at 64x64 / 64 spp took 0.177 s on CPU versus 1.802 s on Metal. Per-sample cost at 64x64 was about 1.7 ms on Metal (occupancy 0.011 to 0.048) versus about 2.4 ms on CPU (occupancy 1). Tested texel coverage was 72%. All values are in the timing table in exact_snippets.

findings.question: Extrapolation: how long would a house atlas of 6 × 2048² at 256 spp take?
findings.answer:
The workload is 6 × 2048² × 256 = 6.44e9 texel-samples at 100% coverage; real atlases reached 59 to 87% coverage in the UV tests.
- CPU (fully occupied): about 8.2e-7 s per covered texel-sample, so about 88 min at 100% coverage or about 66 min at 75%.
- Metal: 5.3 to 7.1e-7 s, measured at only 1 to 5% GPU occupancy, so 57 to 77 min at 100% or 43 to 57 min at 75%. This is an upper bound: at 2048² the GPU would be far better occupied, but full-occupancy throughput could not be measured within the bake-size limits.
- Add about 0.3 to 0.45 s per bake session on Metal (one per object unless meshes are joined), and about 2 s of OIDN RT per 2048² atlas (roughly 12 s total).
- The closed box is a best case; a real house with more triangles and lights will cost more per sample.
- The naive 1.974 s × 6144 ≈ 3.4 h is wrong because it multiplies the fixed per-session overhead.
- Using 64 to 128 spp plus OIDN would cut the total to roughly 11 to 44 min (estimate).

exact_snippets.label: Cycles Metal setup (verified; devices printed)
exact_snippets.content:
sc = bpy.context.scene
sc.render.engine = 'CYCLES'
cp = bpy.context.preferences.addons['cycles'].preferences
cp.compute_device_type = 'METAL'

exact_snippets.label: Lightmap bake call into UV2, in-memory float image (verified)
exact_snippets.content:
mat = bpy.data.materials.new('Room')                 # 5.2: node_tree pre-filled with Principled BSDF + Material Output
tex = mat.node_tree.nodes.new('ShaderNodeTexImage')
mat.node_tree.nodes.active = tex                     # active image node = bake target

lib = ctypes.CDLL(os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(bpy.app.binary_path)), 'Resources', 'lib', 'libOpenImageDenoise.dylib'))

lib.oidnCommitDevice.argtypes = [vp]
lib.oidnGetDeviceError.restype = ctypes.c_int; lib.oidnGetDeviceError.argtypes = [vp, ctypes.POINTER(ctypes.c_char_p)]
lib.oidnGetDeviceInt.restype = ctypes.c_int; lib.oidnGetDeviceInt.argtypes = [vp, ctypes.c_char_p]
lib.oidnNewFilter.restype = vp; lib.oidnNewFilter.argtypes = [vp, ctypes.c_char_p]
lib.oidnSetSharedFilterImage.argtypes = [vp, ctypes.c_char_p, vp, ctypes.c_int, ctypes.c_size_t, ctypes.c_size_t, ctypes.c_size_t, ctypes.c_size_t, ctypes.c_size_t]
lib.oidnSetFilterBool.argtypes = [vp, ctypes.c_char_p, ctypes.c_bool]
lib.oidnCommitFilter.argtypes = [vp]; lib.oidnExecuteFilter.argtypes = [vp]; lib.oidnReleaseFilter.argtypes = [vp]
dev = lib.oidnNewDevice(1)   # 1 = CPU (5 = Metal: creates OK, not executed)
lib.oidnCommitDevice(dev)    # oidnGetDeviceInt(dev, b'version') -> 20500
def oidn_rt(rgba):           # (h, w, 4) float32 from img.pixels
    src = np.ascontiguousarray(rgba, dtype=np.float32); out = np.zeros_like(src); h, w = src.shape[:2]
    f = lib.oidnNewFilter(dev, b'RT')   # b'RTLightmap' -> commit error 3 'unsupported combination of input features'
    lib.oidnSetSharedFilterImage(f, b'color',  src.ctypes.data, 3, w, h, 0, 16, 16 * w)  # 3=OIDN_FORMAT_FLOAT3 read from RGBA stride 16
    lib.oidnSetSharedFilterImage(f, b'output', out.ctypes.data, 3, w, h, 0, 16, 16 * w)
    lib.oidnSetFilterBool(f, b'hdr', True)
    lib.oidnCommitFilter(f); lib.oidnExecuteFilter(f)
    m = ctypes.c_char_p(); err = lib.oidnGetDeviceError(dev, ctypes.byref(m)); lib.oidnReleaseFilter(f)
    if err: raise RuntimeError(m.value)
    out[..., 3] = 1.0
    return out

results.recommendation:
Everything the plan needs from Blender 5.2.1 LTS works headless on this M1. The pipeline should be:

1. **Setup:** use the Metal setup snippet. Always set `cycles.samples` (default 4096) and `use_adaptive_sampling=False` explicitly.
2. **UV2:** give each static mesh a second layer with `uv_layers.new('Lightmap')` and make it the active layer. Pack all meshes of one atlas together, either with `lightmap_pack` (`PACK_IN_ONE`) in object mode or with multi-object edit mode: `smart_project` → `average_islands_scale` → `pack_islands` (margin_method `'FRACTION'`).
3. **Join before baking:** join static geometry per atlas (or bake small props on CPU). Every selected object gets its own Cycles session, costing about 0.26 s on Metal versus 0.03 s on CPU.
4. **Bake:** `DIFFUSE` with pass_filter `{'DIRECT','INDIRECT'}` (no COLOR) into float images, using `uv_layer='Lightmap'`. The margin in pixels must be at least the UV padding.
5. **Denoise:** do it afterwards, in memory, with Blender's bundled OIDN 2.5 via ctypes (RT filter, `hdr=True`). Cycles never denoises bakes, RTLightmap is unavailable, and the compositor Denoise route produced no output headless.
6. **Budget:** plan preview bakes at 512–1024 px with 16–32 spp (seconds to a few minutes). A full 6×2048² bake at 256 spp is a 45–90 min job (upper-bound estimate); 64–128 spp plus OIDN is the likely release setting.

Characters and animation:
- Skeleton mesh + Skin modifier, then `skin_armature_create` under `temp_override`. Alternatively use a custom armature with `parent_set(type='ARMATURE_AUTO')` through view-layer selection.
- Apply Skin/Subsurf in Blender before adding shape keys, because `export_apply=True` blocks shape-key export.
- Author animation only through the layered Action API (slots → layers → strips → `channelbag(slot, ensure=True)` → `fcurves.new`).
- Bake IK with `nla.bake(visual_keying=True, clear_constraints=True)` in POSE mode.
- Put each clip on its own single-strip NLA track (the action_slot is auto-assigned) and export with `export_animation_mode='ACTIONS'`. Delete stray actions or set `export_anim_single_armature=False`.

Export settings: GLB with `export_texcoords=True`, which gives UVMap→TEXCOORD_0 and Lightmap→TEXCOORD_1. Leave `export_apply=False` when shape keys exist. Prefer `EXT_meshopt_compression` (the default) or Draco, pending a three.js-side check.

Blender's bundled Inter/DejaVu woff2 fonts (OFL / Bitstream Vera) and the CC0 hair and geometry-node assets may be used, since they ship with the install. Before the build, run one small test that saves a lightmap to disk (EXR half/HDR/PNG16) and one tiny glTF export; both were deliberately untested here.
risks: glTF exporter behaviour was verified from the 5.2.40 source only; no export was run, per the rules. This covers TEXCOORD_i per UV layer, the ACTIONS-mode NLA gathering, the export_apply/shape-key conflict and Draco/meshopt availability. One tiny export should confirm it at build time.
Saving images to disk was never exercised: image.save / save_render with OPEN_EXR half + codec, HDR, 16-bit PNG or AVIF. This is the one untested link in the lightmap chain.

GPU full-occupancy bake throughput could not be measured within the ≤64² (one 128²@64) limits. The Metal figures ran at 1–5% occupancy, so the extrapolation is an upper bound. A real house (more triangles, many lights, emissive or glossy surfaces) will cost more per sample than the closed test box.
Each selected object gets its own Cycles bake session, costing about 0.26 s on Metal (about 0.027 s on CPU). Baking hundreds of separate objects on the GPU adds minutes, so join meshes per atlas.

The Blender-bundled OIDN lacks RTLightmap weights ('unsupported combination of input features'). The generic RT filter can bleed across UV-island borders and empty texels, so dilate with a bake margin before denoising. Albedo/normal auxiliary inputs in texel space are untested.

The ctypes OIDN route depends on Blender.app/Contents/Resources/lib/libOpenImageDenoise.dylib and the OIDN 2.x C ABI (version 20500); a Blender update could move or change it. The OIDN Metal device (type 5) was created but never executed.
The compositor Denoise route did not work headless: render.render returned in 0.17 s and 'Viewer Node' stayed 256x256 of zeros. Do not rely on it without further work.
export_anim_single_armature=True (the default) exports every bone-animating action in bpy.data.actions when there is a single armature. Stray or test actions will become glTF animations.
export_apply=True prevents exporting shape keys. Skin/Subsurf characters with morph targets need their modifiers applied in Blender before shape keys are authored.

Legacy Action APIs are gone: action.fcurves raises AttributeError, and old tutorials' action.fcurves / groups / id_root code breaks. The exporter reads only the first layer and first strip of each action. NLA strips without an action_slot, and tracks with more than one non-muted strip, are silently skipped (with a log warning).

5.x API breaks: Material.use_nodes is deprecated (removal in 6.0); Scene.node_tree was removed in favour of scene.compositing_node_group; the Boolean solver 'FAST' is now 'FLOAT' (plus 'MANIFOLD'); CurveProfile has no 'CUSTOM' preset, and custom points need curve.update_tag() before the geometry updates.
Cycles GPU bakes are not bit-exact from run to run (max difference 3.6e-7), so exact-equality checks in build scripts will fail.

The Metal kernels are currently cached in ~/.cache/cycles/kernels/Apple_M1. After a Blender update or cache wipe, the first Metal bake may compile kernels for minutes, well beyond a 60 s per-run budget.
8 GB RAM: a 2048² float RGBA image is 64 MB in Blender, plus Cycles bake buffers. Memory for several 2048² atlases in one process was not measured; baking one atlas per Blender process is safer.
M1 has no hardware ray tracing ('Hardware Ray-Tracing: Off'). For tiny bakes the CPU beats Metal because of fixed per-session GPU overhead.

Exporter option export_meshopt_extension offers KHR_meshopt_compression, but whether three.js r186's GLTFLoader/MeshoptDecoder supports the KHR variant was not checked here. EXT_meshopt_compression (the default) is the safer choice until the three.js topic confirms.

results.topic: three.js r186 (three@0.186.1) runtime rendering path: WebGPURenderer + RenderPipeline/TSL for a dark, flashlight-lit horror game with Blender-baked lightmaps, runtime procedural textures, desktop M1 7-core GPU at 2560x1600 Retina

findings.question: Q1a. Minimal RenderPipeline with MRT + TRAA/TAAU: how do I render at a lower internal resolution and upscale over time?
findings.answer: Checked in the r186 files webgpu_upscaling_taau.html and webgpu_postprocessing_traa.html. Pattern: rp = new THREE.RenderPipeline(renderer); scenePass = pass(scene, camera); scenePass.setMRT(mrt({ output, velocity })). Then color = scenePass.getTextureNode('output'), depth = scenePass.getTextureNode('depth') and vel = scenePass.getTextureNode('velocity'). Depth needs no MRT entry. TRAA: traa(color, depth, vel, camera) from three/addons/tsl/display/TRAANode.js; it also has a .useSubpixelCorrection flag. TAAU: lower the input with scenePass.setResolutionScale(s), where the example range is 0.25-1 and the default is 0.5. Then call taau(color, depth, vel, camera) from three/addons/tsl/display/TAAUNode.js. The history and resolve targets are sized to the drawing buffer, so output size = setSize x pixelRatio. It resolves with a 9-tap Blackman-Harris filter. JSDoc: 'Note: MSAA must be disabled when TAAU is in use.' Optional sharpening: sharpen(taauNode.getTextureNode(), 0.2) from SharpenNode.js; change it at runtime with .sharpness.value. Call rp.render() in the loop; rp.renderAsync() has been deprecated since r181. After swapping rp.outputNode, set rp.needsUpdate = true. setResolutionScale can change at runtime (the example GUI does this), so dynamic resolution is possible. TAAU has tuning values (JSDoc defaults: history depth threshold 0.0005, edge depth 0.001, velocity limit 128 px, current-frame weight 0.025). Read the property names from TAAUNode.js during the build.

findings.question: Q1b. FSR1 sharpen/upscale
findings.answer: Checked in webgpu_upscaling_fsr1.html: scenePass.setResolutionScale(0.5); fsr1Node = fsr1(scenePass); rp.outputNode = fsr1Node. The renderer is created with antialias: true because FSR1 needs an anti-aliased source. Signature: fsr1(textureNode, sharpness = 0.2, denoise = false). Sharpness 0 = maximum and 2 = none. It runs 2 passes: EASU at output size, then RCAS. Correct import: 'three/addons/tsl/display/FSR1Node.js'. The file's own @three_import JSDoc wrongly says 'tsl/display/fsr1/FSR1Node.js'. The JSDoc also says: 'Only use FSR 1 if your application is fragment-shader bound' and that FSR1 does not use textureGather yet, which WebGL2 lacks.

findings.question: Q1c. GTAO: what it needs and how it composites
findings.answer: From webgpu_postprocessing_ao.html. It uses a SEPARATE prePass (prePass.transparent = false) with setMRT(mrt({ output: packNormalToRGB(normalView), velocity })). The normal target is set to UnsignedByteType. Normals are read back with prePassNormal = sample(uv => unpackRGBToNormal(prePass.getTextureNode().sample(uv))). aoPass = ao(prePassDepth, prePassNormal, camera) from GTAONode.js. Parameters: .samples/.radius/.scale/.thickness (.value), .resolutionScale (0.5 in the example) and .useTemporalFiltering. The AO is injected into the beauty pass with scenePass.contextNode = builtinAOContext(aoPass.getTextureNode().sample(screenUV).r). That affects only INDIRECT light (the direct flashlight is untouched) and skips transparent materials. TRAA then uses the prePass depth and velocity: traa(scenePass, prePassDepth, prePassVelocity, camera), with scenePass.options.samples = 0. Cost: 2 full geometry passes. A single-pass alternative follows webgpu_postprocessing_ssgi.html: MRT {output, diffuseColor, normal: packNormalToRGB(normalView), velocity}, then multiply AO in post. That also darkens the direct flashlight light.

findings.question: Q1d. Bloom, film grain, chromatic aberration, vignette, tone mapping (AgX/Neutral) and output transform
findings.answer: Bloom: bloom(node, strength = 1, radius = 0, threshold = 0), with runtime uniforms .threshold/.strength/.radius (.value). Example: rp.outputNode = scenePassColor.add(bloomPass). BloomNode also has a resolution-scale setter (around L294). Film: film(inputNode, intensityNode = null, uvNode = null). Chromatic aberration: chromaticAberration(node, strength = 1.0, center = null (screen centre), scale = 1.1). There is no vignette node in r186. The motion-blur example builds one inline: screenUV.distance(.5).remap(.6, 1).mul(2).clamp().oneMinus(). Tone mapping: renderer.toneMapping = THREE.AgXToneMapping (6) or THREE.NeutralToneMapping (7). RenderPipeline.outputColorTransform defaults to true. In that case it wraps outputNode in renderOutput(outputNode, toneMapping, outputColorSpace) at the end. While the inner passes render, it sets renderer.toneMapping = NoToneMapping and the output space to the working colour space, so the passes stay linear HDR. For effects that should run after tone mapping (grain, chromatic aberration, vignette), follow webgpu_postprocessing_ca.html: renderPipeline.outputColorTransform = false; outputPass = renderOutput(scenePass); then chromaticAberration(outputPass, ...). Signature: renderOutput(color, toneMapping = null, outputColorSpace = null).

findings.question: Q1e. Depth of field and motion blur for cutscenes
findings.answer: DoF (webgpu_postprocessing_dof.html): dof(node, viewZNode, focusDistance = 1, focalLength = 1, bokehScale = 1), with viewZNode = scenePass.getViewZNode(). Distances are in world units. The input is wrapped with convertToTexture. Motion blur (webgpu_postprocessing_motion_blur.html): motionBlur(inputNode, velocity, numSamples = int(16)). It is a plain Fn, not a TempNode. It needs scenePass.setMRT(mrt({ output, velocity })) and vel = scenePass.getTextureNode('velocity').mul(blurAmount). Both are ordinary nodes, so turn them on only for cutscenes by swapping rp.outputNode and setting needsUpdate = true.

findings.question: Q1f. What does GodraysNode need and do? What should the flashlight beam use instead?
findings.answer: GodraysNode draws screen-space raymarched godrays: godrays(depthNode, camera, light). JSDoc limits: 'Only point and directional lights are currently supported.' and 'The effect requires a full shadow setup' (renderer.shadowMap.enabled, casters and receivers, light.castShadow). Defaults: resolutionScale 0.5 and uniforms raymarchSteps 60, density 0.7, maxDensity 0.5, distanceAttenuation 2. Composite: bilateralBlur(godraysPassColor), then depthAwareBlend(scenePassColor, blurPassColor, scenePassDepth, camera, { blendColor, edgeRadius, edgeStrength }). It does NOT work with a SpotLight flashlight. For a beam in fog, webgpu_volume_lighting.html (r186) uses a shadow-casting SpotLight with VolumeNodeMaterial: steps = 12, offsetNode = bayer16(screenCoordinate), scatteringNode = Fn(({ positionRay }) => density). The volume mesh sits on its own layer, rendered in a second pass(scene, camera, { depthBuffer: false }) with setLayers and setResolutionScale(.25). depthNode = scenePass depth. It is blurred with gaussianBlur and added to scenePass. There is also a webgpu_volume_lighting_traa.html variant.

findings.question: Q1g. Is SSSNode screen-space shadows?
findings.answer: Yes. SSSNode is Screen-Space Shadows (contact shadows), not subsurface scattering. JSDoc: 'Use Shadow Maps for the foundation and Screen-Space Shadows for the details'. Signature: sss(depthNode, camera, mainLight: DirectionalLight). 'The effect can only be used with a single directional light'. Uniforms: maxDistance 0.1, thickness 0.01, shadowIntensity 1, quality 0.5. Also .resolutionScale = 1 and .useTemporalFiltering, which requires TRAA. It is applied through scenePass.contextNode = builtinShadowContext(sssPass.getTextureNode().sample(screenUV).r, dirLight) (webgpu_postprocessing_sss.html). The ray direction is lightPosition - lightTargetPosition, i.e. parallel rays. Feeding it the flashlight SpotLight would be an unsupported hack. Use it only for a directional moonlight, if one exists.

findings.question: Q1h. Is there a cheaper pipeline without post-processing passes?
findings.answer: Yes: THREE.DirectRenderPipeline, exported from three/webgpu. JSDoc: 'applies output processing directly in material shaders. This avoids the intermediate framebuffer and output pass ... but changes blending and is not compatible with materials that sample the framebuffer, such as transmissive materials.' Example (webgpu_postprocessing_direct.html): rp = new THREE.DirectRenderPipeline(renderer); rp.outputNode = vec4(saturation(output.rgb, f), output.a); rp.render(scene, camera). It cannot do bloom, TAA or other multi-pass effects. It suits a Low preset with MSAA plus per-pixel vignette and grain.

findings.question: Q2a. How does the WebGL2 fallback work (automatic fallback, forceWebGL)?
findings.answer: WebGPURenderer constructor: if parameters.forceWebGL, it uses WebGLBackend ('the renderer uses a WebGL 2 backend no matter if WebGPU is supported or not'). Otherwise it uses WebGPUBackend with getFallback = () => { warn('WebGPURenderer: WebGPU is not available, running under WebGL2 backend.'); return new WebGLBackend(parameters) }. Renderer.init() catches any backend.init error and switches to the fallback. WebGPUBackend.init calls navigator.gpu.requestAdapter({ powerPreference, featureLevel: 'compatibility' }). If navigator.gpu is undefined the call throws; if the adapter is null it throws 'Unable to create WebGPU adapter'. Either way the renderer falls back automatically. After await renderer.init(), check renderer.backend.isWebGPUBackend or renderer.backend.isWebGLBackend. hasFeatureAsync() is deprecated since r181; use hasFeature() after init.

findings.question: Q2b. Which of these nodes work on the WebGL2 backend, and is it viable for a Low preset?
findings.answer: Checked by reading source only; nothing was run. MRT works: WebGLBackend binds attachments with state.drawBuffers. velocity is a plain node with no backend-specific code. TRAA and TAAU contain explicit WebGL-backend handling. TRAA's depth-copy comment says 'This does not happen with the WebGL backend'. TAAU keeps a previous-depth target 'so that copyTextureToTexture can copy into it on the WebGL backend, which uses a framebuffer blit'. FSR1 has a WebGL2 path (no textureGather). GTAO, Bloom, DoF, SSS, Godrays and MotionBlur have no backend checks; they are all QuadMesh render passes, so they should work. LightProbeGrid.bake only checks renderer.isWebGPURenderer, and WebGLBackend supports isRenderTarget3D through framebufferTextureLayer, so it is plausible but not tested. NOT available on WebGL2: compute with StorageTexture/textureStore. StorageTexture.js says: 'can only be used with WebGPURenderer and a WebGPU backend'. GLSLNodeBuilder sets supports.storageBuffer = false. WebGL compute is transform feedback over storage buffer attributes only. webgpu_compute_texture.html guards with WebGPU.isAvailable(). Subgroup builtins are also unsupported. Conclusion: WebGL2 is viable for Low if procedural textures use render-to-texture instead of compute and the post chain stays light. Test with new THREE.WebGPURenderer({ forceWebGL: true }).

findings.question: Q2c. Is WebGPU available in Safari 26 on macOS 15 Sequoia?
findings.answer: Probably not enabled by default. Apple's primary sources do not restrict WebGPU by OS: the Safari 26 release notes say 'Added support for WebGPU. (145801580)' and 'Safari 26 is available for iOS 26, iPadOS 26, visionOS 26, macOS 26, macOS Sequoia, and macOS Sonoma.' WebKit's blog says it is 'now shipping in Safari 26.0 for macOS, iOS, iPadOS, and visionOS'. However, the gpuweb Implementation Status wiki says 'In macOS Tahoe 26, iOS 26, iPadOS 26, and visionOS 26, WebGPU is supported and enabled by default.' caniuse marks Safari 26.x as partial support, note #7: 'only being enabled by default on macOS 26 Tahoe or later' (it can be turned on with the WebGPU feature flag). Practical result: Safari on this Sequoia Mac will most likely use the WebGL2 fallback.

findings.question: Q2d. Is WebGPU available in Firefox on macOS?
findings.answer: Yes, from Firefox 147. MDN Firefox 147 release notes: 'WebGPU API support is now enabled for all macOS versions on devices with Apple Silicon processors (previously only macOS Tahoe support was enabled). (Firefox bug 1993341)'. The gpuweb wiki agrees: Apple Silicon from 145 on macOS 26+, and from 147 on all macOS versions. caniuse note #8 (Tahoe-only) is out of date. On the M1 with macOS 15, Firefox 147+ should use WebGPU.

findings.question: Q3a. Do lightMap and lightMapIntensity work under WebGPURenderer r186, and which UV set is used?
findings.answer: Yes. NodeMaterial.setupLightMap(builder) returns new IrradianceNode(materialLightMap) when material.lightMap is set. materialLightMap = lightMap.rgb * lightMapIntensity (MaterialNode.LIGHT_MAP). It is added to builder.context.irradiance, i.e. indirect diffuse. This covers MeshStandardMaterial (converted automatically) and MeshStandardNodeMaterial; webgpu_materials_lightmap.html changes material.lightMapIntensity live. UV: TextureNode.getDefaultUV() returns uv(this.value.channel), so set lightMapTexture.channel = 1 to read the 'uv1' attribute. GLTFLoader maps TEXCOORD_1 to 'uv1'. There is NO lightMapNode property in r186. Verified NodeMaterial node properties: lightsNode, envNode, aoNode, colorNode, normalNode, opacityNode, backdropNode, backdropAlphaNode, alphaTestNode, maskNode, maskShadowNode, positionNode, geometryNode, depthNode, receivedShadowPositionNode, castShadowPositionNode, receivedShadowNode, castShadowNode, outputNode, mrtNode, fragmentNode, vertexNode, contextNode. MeshStandardNodeMaterial adds emissiveNode, metalnessNode and roughnessNode.

findings.question: Q3b. How do I decode a custom RGBM lightmap and blend base + lightning-flash lightmaps in TSL?
findings.answer: Override setupLightMap(builder) in a MeshStandardNodeMaterial subclass and return new THREE.IrradianceNode(yourNode). IrradianceNode is exported from three/webgpu via nodes/Nodes.js. three itself uses this pattern: MeshBasicNodeMaterial overrides setupLightMap. yourNode = decode(base) + decode(flash) * lightningUniform. Light adds linearly, so an additive flash-only bake is exact. The decode is sampled with texture(tex, uv(1)). r186 has no RGBM helper or loader (no RGBM file in the package), so the encoding is our own convention and the Blender script must match it. Texture flags: channel = 1; flipY = false (glTF UV convention, while TextureLoader/EXRLoader default to true); colorSpace = THREE.NoColorSpace so no sRGB decode corrupts M. 8-bit linear RGBM bands in dark areas, so store sqrt(rgb) or use half-float EXR (EXRLoader and HDRLoader ship in examples/jsm/loaders). This snippet was not run.

findings.question: Q3c. How do AO (GTAO or aoMap) and lightmaps interact?
findings.answer: PhysicalLightingModel.ambientOcclusion multiplies reflectedLight.indirectDiffuse by ambientOcclusion, and indirectSpecular by a roughness-based term. Lightmap irradiance lands in indirectDiffuse, so GTAO through builtinAOContext darkens the lightmaps a second time, even though Cycles bakes already contain occlusion. The getAO context callback receives the material (builtinAOContext: getAO: (inputNode, { material }) => ...). So a custom context(null, { getAO }) on scenePass can skip or weaken AO for materials with material.userData.lightmapped. Keeping about 30-40% AO there preserves contact darkening where characters meet lightmapped floors. builtinGIContext(aoNode, giNode) also exists (getAO + getGI).

findings.question: Q4. Light probes for dynamic objects: what exists in r186, and how should characters get lighting that matches the lightmaps?
findings.answer: The r186 file list has: examples/jsm/lighting/LightProbeGrid.js (WebGPURenderer version), LightProbeGridWebGL.js (for WebGLRenderer) and LightProbeGridUtils.js; tsl/lighting/LightProbeGridNode.js; helpers/LightProbeGridHelper.js and LightProbeGridHelperWebGL.js; lights/LightProbeGenerator.js; helpers/LightProbeHelper(GPU).js; src/lights/LightProbe.js; src/nodes/lighting/LightProbeNode.js; IrradianceNode.js; functions/material/getShIrradianceAt.js. There is no class named IrradianceVolume. LightProbeGrid is a grid of L2 spherical-harmonic irradiance probes stored in one RGBA RenderTarget3D atlas (7 sub-volumes). It extends Light, so adding it to the scene lights every lit node material automatically. API: new LightProbeGrid(width, height, depth, widthProbes?, heightProbes?, depthProbes?). The volume is centred on .position. Other members: .falloff (default 0), .intensity, .texture, getProbePosition(), updateBoundingBox(), dispose(). bake(renderer, scene, { cubemapSize = 8, near = 0.1, far = 100, bounces = 0, sampleCount = 512, start = 0, count, pass = 0 }). The bake is fully on the GPU using CubeCamera, QuadMesh and RenderTarget3D, with no CPU readback. Example: await probes.bake(renderer, scene, { cubemapSize: 32, near: 0.05, far: 20 }); scene.add(probes). Recommendation: at load, bake the grid from the lightmapped static scene with the flashlight and characters hidden and bounces: 0 (the lightmaps already contain bounced light). Characters then get grid irradiance plus the dynamic flashlight. Keep the grid OFF lightmapped surfaces with material.lightsNode = lights([flashlight, ...]) (webgpu_lights_selective.html pattern), otherwise indirect light is counted twice. For lightning, bake a second grid while showing only the flash lightmap and drive its .intensity with the same uniform. If scene.environment is set, it still reaches lightmapped materials; for this game, use no scene.environment.

findings.question: Q5. Shadows under WebGPU r186: map types, SpotLight.map (cookie), radius/blur and costs
findings.answer: Shadow map types: BasicShadowMap (0); PCFShadowMap (1, the default for renderer.shadowMap.type); PCFSoftShadowMap has been REMOVED; VSMShadowMap (3). With PCFSoftShadowMap, Renderer warns 'WebGPURenderer: PCFSoftShadowMap has been removed. Using PCFShadowMap instead.' The ShadowNode filter table lists null /* PCFSoftShadowMap, removed */. PCF takes 5 Vogel-disk taps scaled by shadow.radius (a per-shadow reference); with hardware compare it uses a linear-filtered depth texture, otherwise nearest. VSM does not apply to point lights and adds 2 blur passes (vertical and horizontal, RG HalfFloat targets) driven by shadow.radius and shadow.blurSamples. Light cookie: SpotLightNode supports light.map (texture) AND light.colorNode = (lightCoord) => node, a procedural TSL cookie. The projection uses lightShadowMatrix, which updates the shadow matrices even when castShadow is false or shadowMap is disabled, so cookies work without shadows. ProjectorLight (three/webgpu) is a SpotLight variant with .aspect. Example webgpu_lights_spotlight.html: spotLight.map, castShadow, shadow.mapSize 1024, shadow.focus. Costs (reasoned, not measured): each shadowed SpotLight re-renders its casters every frame into a mapSize-squared depth map; a PointLight renders 6 faces; VSM adds 2 fullscreen passes over the map; PCF costs 5 compare taps per lit fragment.

findings.question: Q6a. Runtime procedural textures: compute into StorageTexture, or render-to-texture? Mipmaps? What works on WebGL2?
findings.answer: Render-to-texture works on BOTH backends. convertToTexture(node, w, h) and rtt(node, w, h, options) build an RTTNode, which creates new RenderTarget(w, h, { type: HalfFloatType, ...options }). Options include autoUpdate (set false for render-once), generateMipmaps and minFilter (RenderTarget options; default generateMipmaps = false). Both backends generate render-target mipmaps in finishRender when texture.generateMipmaps === true (WebGPUBackend around L1578, WebGLBackend around L572). Caveat: an RTTNode only renders from updateBefore while it is part of a rendered node graph. To bake a standalone Texture once, use new THREE.RenderTarget(...) + new THREE.QuadMesh(material); renderer.setRenderTarget(rt); quad.render(renderer); renderer.setRenderTarget(null). The compute path works on the WebGPU backend ONLY: new THREE.StorageTexture(w, h), textureStore(tex, uvec2, vec4).toWriteOnly() inside Fn(...).compute(w*h), then renderer.compute(node) after await renderer.init() (webgpu_compute_texture.html). StorageTexture.mipmapsAutoUpdate = true (default) regenerates mips after compute writes. Recommendation: one render-to-texture baker (RenderTarget + QuadMesh) for all presets and both backends. Render once at the preset's resolution with generateMipmaps plus LinearMipmapLinearFilter and RepeatWrapping, then dispose the generator materials.

findings.question: Q6b. Which TSL noise functions exist in r186, with signatures?
findings.answer: Read from src/nodes/materialx/MaterialXNodes.js and exported through three/tsl: mx_noise_float, mx_noise_vec3 and mx_noise_vec4 (texcoord = uv(), amplitude = 1, pivot = 0) are Perlin. mx_fractal_noise_float, _vec2, _vec3 and _vec4 (position = uv(), octaves = 3, lacunarity = 2, diminish = .5, amplitude = 1), plus mx_fractal_noise_float_2d. mx_worley_noise_float (texcoord = uv(), jitter = 1, style = 0), plus _float_2d and _float_3d. mx_worley_noise_vec2 (texcoord, jitter); mx_worley_noise_vec3 (texcoord, jitter, metric = 1); mx_worley_noise_vec3_style (texcoord, jitter, style = 0, metric = 0). mx_cell_noise_float and mx_cell_noise_vec3 (texcoord = uv()). mx_unifiednoise2d and 3d (noiseType, texcoord, freq, offset, jitter = 1, outmin = 0, outmax = 1, clampoutput = false, octaves = 1, lacunarity = 2, diminish = .5, style = 0), where noiseType 0 = perlin, 1 = cell, 2 = worley, 3 = fractal. Also mx_heighttonormal, mx_ramp*/mx_split*, mx_hsvtorgb and mx_rgbtohsv. Core: triNoise3D(position, speed, time), interleavedGradientNoise and hash. Addons: tsl/math/curlNoise.js (permute, snoise(vec3), snoiseVec3, curlNoise(p)); tsl/math/voronoiNoise.js (hash2d, voronoi2d(p, time), hash3d, voronoi3d(p, time)); tsl/math/Bayer.js (bayer16); tsl/utils/RNoise.js (bindAnalyticNoise(resolution, seed = 0)). The mx_* functions take no period parameter, so textures baked from them will NOT tile seamlessly; write periodic noise in TSL (wrap lattice cells with mod(period)) for tileable textures.

findings.question: Q7. Loading: GLTFLoader + MeshoptDecoder, shader precompilation, memory stats
findings.answer: GLTFLoader supports KHR_draco_mesh_compression (setDRACOLoader), EXT_meshopt_compression (setMeshoptDecoder), KHR_mesh_quantization, KHR_texture_transform and KHR_materials_emissive_strength; it has loadAsync and parseAsync. The meshopt decoder ships in the package: examples/jsm/libs/meshopt_decoder.module.js with export { MeshoptDecoder } (.ready, .supported). Only the decoder ships (plus meshopt_simplifier and meshopt_clusterizer modules); there is no encoder. DRACOLoader r186 resolves its decoder files locally through new URL('../libs/draco/...', import.meta.url), and DRACO_GLTF_CONFIG = { js: '../libs/draco/gltf/draco_wasm_wrapper.js', wasm: '../libs/draco/gltf/draco_decoder.wasm' }, used as dracoLoader.setDecoderPath(DRACO_GLTF_CONFIG). No CDN is needed. Precompile: await renderer.init(), then await renderer.compileAsync(scene, camera, targetScene = null, onProgress = null), which compiles scene materials. RenderPipeline has no compile method and renderAsync is deprecated, so render one or two warm-up frames behind the loading screen. Memory stats: renderer.info.memory has attributes, attributesSize, geometries, indexAttributes(Size), indirectStorageAttributes(Size), programs, programsSize, readbackBuffers(Size), renderTargets, storageAttributes(Size), textures, texturesSize, uniformBuffers(Size) and total. info.render has calls, frameCalls, drawCalls, triangles, points, lines and timestamp; info.compute has calls, frameCalls and timestamp. renderer.resolveTimestampsAsync(type = 'render') also exists. Not checked (Blender was not run): Blender's exporter can write Draco but not meshopt.

findings.question: Q8. Animation: AnimationMixer/crossFadeTo, makeClipAdditive + subclip, CCDIKSolver
findings.answer: AnimationAction has play, stop, reset, setLoop, setEffectiveWeight, fadeIn, fadeOut, crossFadeFrom(fadeOutAction, duration, warp = false), crossFadeTo(fadeInAction, duration, warp = false), setEffectiveTimeScale, syncWith and warp. AnimationUtils.subclip(sourceClip, name, startFrame, endFrame, fps = 30) and AnimationUtils.makeClipAdditive(targetClip, referenceFrame = 0, referenceClip = targetClip, fps = 30) exist as both named and static exports. CCDIKSolver import: 'three/addons/animation/CCDIKSolver.js'. new CCDIKSolver(skinnedMesh, iks = []); update(globalBlendFactor = 1.0); updateOne(ik, overrideBlend = 1.0); createHelper(sphereSize); CCDIKHelper. The JSDoc types limitation, rotationMin and rotationMax as numbers, but the code reads limitation.x/.y/.z (an axis Vector3) and clamps with Vector3 max/min, so pass THREE.Vector3 values. Call solver.update() after mixer.update(dt).

findings.question: Q9. Recommended renderer path and post chain per preset for an M1 7-core GPU on a 2560x1600 Retina display
findings.answer:
All numbers are unbenchmarked starting points. Display math: at the default 'looks like 1440x900', window.devicePixelRatio = 2, and every example calls setPixelRatio(window.devicePixelRatio), which gives a 2880x1800 (5.2 MP) drawing buffer. Every preset must cap setPixelRatio, and TAAU's output equals that drawing buffer. Use THREE.WebGPURenderer everywhere; Safari on Sequoia falls back to WebGL2 automatically.

LOW (WebGL2-safe):
- pixelRatio 1, giving 1440x900 (1.3 MP); go to 0.75 (1080x675) if slow.
- antialias: true (MSAA 4x) with DirectRenderPipeline, which puts vignette, cheap hash grain and tone mapping in the material shaders.
- No TAA, GTAO, bloom or volumetrics.
- Flashlight: PCF 1024 shadows, radius 1-2, texture cookie.
- LightProbeGrid baked with cubemapSize 8; procedural textures 512-1024 via render-to-texture.

MEDIUM (default on M1 with WebGPU):
- pixelRatio 1 (1440x900 output), antialias: false.
- scenePass.setResolutionScale(0.75), giving 1080x675 (0.73 MP) internal.
- Chain: MRT{output, velocity} -> TAAU -> sharpen 0.2 -> bloom (high threshold) -> renderOutput (AgX) -> subtle CA x vignette -> film grain.
- Flashlight PCF 1024-2048; optional volumetric beam at 0.25 scale with 8 steps.
- Textures 1024-2048.

MAX:
- pixelRatio 1.5 (2160x1350, 2.9 MP output); scene and prePass resolution scale 0.667, giving 1440x900 internal.
- prePass MRT{normal as UnsignedByte, velocity} -> GTAO (resolutionScale 0.5, temporal on, lightmap-aware getAO).
- Then scenePass -> TAAU -> sharpen -> bloom -> renderOutput -> CA -> vignette -> film, plus a VolumeNodeMaterial flashlight beam at 0.25 scale.
- DoF and motion blur only during cutscenes.
- Flashlight PCF 2048; textures 2048 (4096 only for hero surfaces, watch the 8 GB).

All presets: add dynamic resolution by adjusting setResolutionScale from frame time.

results.recommendation:
Use `THREE.WebGPURenderer` from `three/webgpu` for every preset. After `await renderer.init()`, check `renderer.backend.isWebGPUBackend`. Safari 26 on this Sequoia Mac will most likely end up on the WebGL2 fallback, so Low must be designed and tested with `forceWebGL: true`.

1. **Pixel ratio:** cap `setPixelRatio` in every preset. Low and Medium use 1 (1440x900); Max uses 1.5 (2160x1350). Never use `window.devicePixelRatio`, which gives 2880x1800 here.
2. **Low:**
   - `antialias: true` (MSAA 4x) with `DirectRenderPipeline`. Vignette, a cheap grain and AgX/Neutral tone mapping run inside the material shaders.
   - Flashlight: PCF 1024 shadows with a texture cookie.
   - No TAA, GTAO, bloom or volumetrics.
3. **Medium:**
   - `RenderPipeline`: `pass()` at resolution scale 0.75 (1080x675) with MRT {output, velocity}.
   - Then TAAU, sharpen 0.2, bloom, `renderOutput` (with `outputColorTransform = false`), subtle chromatic aberration times vignette, and film grain.
4. **Max:** internal scale 0.667 (1440x900 into 2160x1350).
   - Adds a prePass for GTAO at 0.5 scale, using a custom `getAO` context that only weakly darkens lightmapped surfaces.
   - Adds a `VolumeNodeMaterial` flashlight beam at 0.25 scale and PCF 2048 shadows.
   - Depth of field and motion blur are swapped in for cutscenes only (change `rp.outputNode`, then set `needsUpdate`).
5. **Lighting:**
   - Blender lightmaps go through a `MeshStandardNodeMaterial` subclass that overrides `setupLightMap()` and returns `new THREE.IrradianceNode(base + flash * uniform)`. Lightmap textures need `channel = 1`, `flipY = false` and `NoColorSpace`. Use sqrt-encoded RGBM or half-float EXR so dark areas don't band.
   - Characters are lit by a `LightProbeGrid` baked at load from the lightmapped scene (`bounces: 0`, flashlight and characters hidden), plus the flashlight.
   - Keep the grid off lightmapped materials with `material.lightsNode = lights([flashlight])`.
   - Use a second grid for the lightning flash, with its `.intensity` driven by the same uniform.
6. **Flashlight:** a `SpotLight` with a cookie via `.map`, or a procedural `.colorNode(lightCoord)`. Don't plan on `GodraysNode` or `SSSNode` for it; they only take directional or point lights, and SSS is directional only.
7. **Procedural textures:** one bake path for all presets and both backends: `RenderTarget` + `QuadMesh`, rendered once at the preset size (512–1024 / 1024–2048 / 2048). Use `generateMipmaps` and `LinearMipmapLinearFilter`. Write periodic TSL noise so textures tile, since the `mx_*` functions have no period.
8. **Loading:** `GLTFLoader` + `DRACOLoader(DRACO_GLTF_CONFIG)`, which uses local decoder files. Then `compileAsync` plus one or two warm-up `rp.render()` calls behind the loading screen. Watch `renderer.info.memory` against the 8 GB of RAM.
9. **Benchmark:** every resolution and frame-rate number here is a starting point. Measure on this M1 in Chrome and Firefox (WebGPU) and in Safari (WebGL2) before fixing the presets.
risks: Safari 26 on macOS 15 Sequoia most likely runs WebGPU only behind a feature flag, according to caniuse and the gpuweb wiki; Apple's own sources don't say either way. So Safari will use the WebGL2 backend, where compute and StorageTexture are unavailable. All must-have content, especially procedural textures, needs a render-to-texture path.

Nothing about the WebGL2 backend was run. MRT, TRAA, TAAU, GTAO and FSR1 support is based only on reading the source, and so is LightProbeGrid.bake writing into a RenderTarget3D on WebGL2. Test early with forceWebGL: true.

Retina trap: copying setPixelRatio(window.devicePixelRatio) from the examples gives a 2880x1800 buffer (5.2 MP) on this machine, which is too much for a 7-core M1. TAAU's output size follows the drawing buffer, so cap the pixel ratio before tuning resolution scale.

Lighting counted twice: GTAO (via builtinAOContext) multiplies indirect diffuse, which includes the lightmap. LightProbeGrid also adds to every lit material. Without a custom getAO context and material.lightsNode = lights([...]) on lightmapped materials, static surfaces get double occlusion and double indirect light.

Lightmap texture pitfalls: a missing texture.channel = 1 reads UV0; flipY defaults to true in TextureLoader/EXRLoader; SRGBColorSpace corrupts the RGBM M channel. 8-bit linear RGBM bands badly in a dark game, so use sqrt/gamma encoding or half-float EXR.

GTAO in r186 is designed around a second geometry prePass (depth, normals, velocity), roughly doubling vertex and draw cost. Combining a prePass with TAAU has no official example; only the TRAA + prePass combination is shown. Treat Max-preset GTAO as optional.

GodraysNode supports only point and directional lights and needs full shadows; SSSNode supports only one directional light. Neither fits the flashlight. Beam effects need VolumeNodeMaterial (an extra pass plus a shadowed SpotLight).
The mx_* noise functions have no period parameter, so textures baked from them will show seams when tiled. Periodic noise must be written in TSL.
RTTNode only renders while it is part of a rendered node graph (updateBefore). Baking to a standalone Texture needs the explicit RenderTarget + QuadMesh path.
Temporal AA (TRAA/TAAU) can ghost with a fast-moving flashlight hotspot and with animated grain. Apply film grain after TAAU/renderOutput, never before.

Doc/code mismatches in r186: FSR1Node's @three_import path is wrong (the real path is tsl/display/FSR1Node.js). CCDIKSolver's JSDoc types limitation/rotationMin/rotationMax as numbers, but the code needs Vector3. PCFSoftShadowMap has been removed and falls back to PCF. VSM does not apply to point lights.

DRACOLoader finds its decoder files through new URL(..., import.meta.url) inside node_modules. Check that Vite dev and build resolve the wasm. The fallback is to copy examples/jsm/libs/draco/gltf/* into public/ and call setDecoderPath('/draco/'). Blender's exporter support for Draco but not meshopt was NOT checked, because Blender was not run.

Every preset resolution and frame-rate figure is an unbenchmarked estimate. The 8 GB of unified memory limits HalfFloat MRT targets, TAAU history buffers and 2048-4096 procedural textures, so watch renderer.info.memory.
RenderPipeline has no compile API and renderAsync is deprecated, so the post-chain shaders compile on the first rp.render(). Do warm-up renders during loading to avoid a hitch.

results.topic: Pre-download device detection (raw WebGL2 + navigator.gpu only), preset recommendation (Low/Medium/Max), FPS counter, and rAF frame cap, for a three.js r186 desktop horror game. Evidence comes from current browser/engine sources, specs, BCD and the dev M1. The sketches below are UNTESTED.

findings.question: Q1 Chrome/Edge (macOS): UNMASKED_RENDERER_WEBGL today
findings.answer: Blink passes the raw ANGLE GL_RENDERER through unfiltered when WEBGL_debug_renderer_info is enabled. Plain gl.RENDERER returns 'WebKit WebGL' and gl.VENDOR returns 'WebKit'. ANGLE builds the string as 'ANGLE (<vendor>, <backend renderer>, <version>)' and strips commas from each part. The Metal renderer part is 'ANGLE Metal Renderer: ' + MTLDevice.name. For WebGL contexts the version is always 'Unspecified Version', and vendor id 0x106B maps to 'Apple'. So this M1 in Chrome shows 'ANGLE (Apple, ANGLE Metal Renderer: Apple M1, Unspecified Version)'. Pro/Max/Ultra chips also come through MTLDevice.name (e.g. 'Apple M1 Pro'), but I did not observe those names this session, so the regex must be tolerant. Current Blink source has no masking or deprecation of the extension.

findings.question: Q1 Chrome/Edge (Windows): renderer string format
findings.answer: With the ANGLE D3D11 backend the renderer part is '<DXGI adapter description> (<hex deviceId>) Direct3D11[on12] vs_5_0 ps_5_0' and the WebGL version is 'D3D11'. Example: 'ANGLE (NVIDIA, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 (0x00002504) Direct3D11 vs_5_0 ps_5_0, D3D11)'. The format is verified from ANGLE source. The concrete device names and hex padding are illustrative, not observed.

findings.question: Q1 Safari (macOS/iOS): UNMASKED_RENDERER_WEBGL
findings.answer: WebKit hardcodes UNMASKED_RENDERER_WEBGL = 'Apple GPU' and UNMASKED_VENDOR_WEBGL = 'Apple Inc.'. This applies to every Mac, including Intel and AMD-dGPU Macs, and to iOS. There is no model and no core count. The string is useless for tiering, so the decision falls to the WebGPU vendor plus the benchmark.

findings.question: Q1 Firefox (macOS/Windows): renderer masking and deprecation
findings.answer:
Firefox returns the same SanitizeRenderer() bucket plus the suffix ', or similar' from both UNMASKED_RENDERER_WEBGL and plain gl.RENDERER. The relevant prefs default on: webgl.sanitize-unmasked-renderer=true and webgl.enable-renderer-query=true. gl.VENDOR is 'Mozilla', and with resistFingerprinting the renderer becomes 'Mozilla'. The buckets:
- Any renderer starting with 'Apple' becomes 'Apple M1', so every Apple-silicon Mac reports 'Apple M1, or similar'.
- GeForce 900 and newer (including RTX 3060 and 4090) become 'GeForce GTX 980'.
- RX cards, Vega, RENOIR and REMBRANDT become 'Radeon R9 200 Series'. That means Vega APUs land in the same bucket as an RX 6700 XT.
- A generic 'AMD Radeon(TM) Graphics' becomes 'Radeon HD 3200 Graphics'.
- Intel iGPUs without a model number (e.g. Iris Xe) become 'Intel(R) HD Graphics'; UHD 620 becomes 'Intel(R) HD Graphics 400'.
- Any Arc becomes 'Intel(R) Arc(TM) A750 Graphics'.
- Windows ANGLE strings keep their shape, e.g. 'ANGLE (NVIDIA, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 980 Direct3D11 vs_5_0 ps_5_0), or similar' (derived by applying the regexes, not observed).
BCD marks the extension deprecated in Firefox (bug 1722782). A third-party sample of 1000 macOS Firefox users had 951 reporting 'Apple M1, or similar'. In Firefox, treat the string as a vendor hint only.

findings.question: Q1 WebGPU adapter.info in Chrome
findings.answer:
Chrome exposes vendor, architecture, subgroupMinSize/MaxSize and isFallbackAdapter. device and description stay empty unless the WebGPU Developer Features flag is on. Names are Dawn js_enum_case: vendor is 'apple', 'nvidia', 'intel' or 'amd'. Architecture values:
- Intel: 'gen-9', 'gen-11', 'gen-12lp' (Iris Xe), 'gen-12hp', 'xe-lpg', 'xe-2lpg', …
- AMD: 'gcn-5', 'rdna-2', …
- NVIDIA: 'turing', 'ampere', 'lovelace', 'blackwell'.
- Apple (no device id): 'metal-3' on macOS 13+ if the Metal3 family is supported, else 'common-3/2/1'. This gives no chip model.
The hyphenation above is derived from the generator code; normalize by stripping non-alphanumerics before matching. Availability: Chrome 113 (macOS/Windows/ChromeOS), Linux from 144 (Intel Gen12+ only), Android 121, and adapter.info since 127.

findings.question: Q1 WebGPU adapter.info in Safari 26
findings.answer: Traced in WebKit: MTLDevice.name → wgpuAdapterGetInfo(info.name) → GPUAdapter::name() → GPUAdapterInfo. vendor() is the first word of that name, lowercased with non-alphanumerics removed. architecture(), device() and description() all return the same value as vendor(), and isFallbackAdapter is always false. Expected result is 'apple' on Apple silicon. On Intel or AMD Macs it would be something like 'intelr' or 'amd' (inferred, not observed). This is the only raw-API way to tell Apple-silicon Macs from Intel Macs in Safari.

findings.question: Q1 WebGPU adapter.info in Firefox
findings.answer: GetVendor, GetArchitecture, GetDevice and GetDescription all return empty strings. subgroupMin/Max are 4/128. isFallbackAdapter reflects whether wgpu reports a CPU device. Per BCD, WebGPU ships on Windows in 141, on macOS Tahoe (Apple silicon) in 145, and on older macOS (Apple silicon) in 147. It is not available on Intel Macs or Linux.

findings.question: Q2 navigator.deviceMemory
findings.answer: Chromium only (Chrome 63+). Firefox and Safari return undefined. Chromium rounds physical RAM to the nearest power of two and clamps it to 2–32 GB on desktop and 1–8 GB on Android. BCD: from Chrome 147 the values are 2/4/8/16/32; before 147 they were 0.25–8, so '8' on Chrome <147 means '≥8'. Use it only as a lower-bound cap. This 8 GB M1 reports 8.

findings.question: Q2 hardwareConcurrency
findings.answer: Chrome and Firefox report logical CPUs (Firefox caps at the pref dom.maxHardwareConcurrency=128). Safari reports 4 if the machine has fewer than 8 cores, otherwise 8; with advanced privacy protections it reports 8 or 4. So Safari cannot tell an M1 (8 cores) from an M1 Pro/Max. This M1 has hw.ncpu=8, so it reports 8 everywhere.

findings.question: Q2 userAgentData, pointer media queries, iPad
findings.answer: navigator.userAgentData is Chromium only: .mobile since Chrome 90, .platform since 93. Since Chrome 144, getHighEntropyValues is governed by the ch-ua-high-entropy-values permissions policy. Firefox and Safari don't have it. The '(pointer: coarse)' and '(any-pointer: fine)' media queries are supported in Chrome 41, Firefox 64 and Safari 9. Treating a Mac user agent with maxTouchPoints > 1 as an iPad in desktop mode is a heuristic I did not verify.

findings.question: Q2 screen size and devicePixelRatio on this dev Mac
findings.answer: system_profiler reports a 2560x1600 Retina panel, UI 'looks like' 1440 x 900 @ 60.00Hz, backing store 2880 x 1800, 7 GPU cores and Metal 3. Chrome and Safari are installed; Firefox is not. So the browser should report screen 1440x900 CSS px with DPR 2, i.e. 2880x1800 = 5.18 MP. That is 26% more than 2560x1600. The panel is 60 Hz, not ProMotion. The browser values are inferred, not executed. The resolution math must use screen.width*dpr, not the panel size.

findings.question: Q3 context attributes: failIfMajorPerformanceCaveat and powerPreference
findings.answer: Per the spec, failIfMajorPerformanceCaveat:true makes context creation fail when performance would be 'dramatically lower than that of a native application', e.g. a software rasterizer. Try it first; if it fails but a normal context works, set the preset to Low and warn. three r186 WebGLRenderer defaults to powerPreference='default' and failIfMajorPerformanceCaveat=false. The game must pass the same powerPreference the benchmark used ('high-performance'). Otherwise a dual-GPU laptop gets benchmarked on one GPU and plays on the other.

findings.question: Q3 GPU sync for the micro-benchmark (vsync-free)
findings.answer: The WebGL2 spec lets the clientWaitSync timeout be capped at an implementation-defined MAX_CLIENT_WAIT_TIMEOUT_WEBGL, which may be 0, and a larger timeout is INVALID_OPERATION. Sync objects only signal after control returns to the event loop, and query results likewise. A single setTimeout(0) or rAF is not guaranteed to be enough. So end each batch with a 1x1 gl.readPixels from the offscreen FBO, which blocks until the batch finishes. The non-blocking alternative is fenceSync(SYNC_GPU_COMMANDS_COMPLETE, 0) polled via getSyncParameter(SYNC_STATUS) across setTimeout ticks. Render only into an FBO and never present or use rAF during the benchmark, so vsync never applies.

findings.question: Q3 EXT_disjoint_timer_query_webgl2 availability
findings.answer: Available in Chrome desktop 70+ and Edge 80+. Not in Chrome Android or Safari. Firefox gates it behind webgl.enable-privileged-extensions, which defaults to false, so web pages can't use it. Feature-detect it and use it only as an optional cross-check or dev overlay, never as the primary timer.

findings.question: Q3 watchdog limits
findings.answer: Windows TdrDelay defaults to 2 seconds. Keep every single draw far below that (the sketch aborts when one draw takes more than 50 ms) and grow the batch size instead. Also handle webglcontextlost and gl.isContextLost().

findings.question: Q3 benchmark algorithm and scoring (design)
findings.answer:
1. Use a detached 1x1 canvas and a WebGL2 context with {powerPreference:'high-performance', antialias:false, depth:false, stencil:false, alpha:false}.
2. Render a 512x512 RGBA8 FBO with a fullscreen triangle (gl_VertexID, no attributes). The fragment shader runs an ALU loop of sin/cos/fract with a uniform iteration count (64) and a per-draw random uSeed, which prevents unrolling, constant folding and dead-code elimination.
3. Warm up with one draw to cover shader/pipeline compile.
4. Double the draws per batch until one batch takes ≥40 ms (the timer has about 1 ms precision).
5. Discard everything in the first ~300 ms (compile plus GPU clock ramp-up) and yield between batches.
6. Take the median per-draw time over a total budget of about 1.5 s.
7. Raw score = Mpix·iter/ms. Score = 100·raw/REF[browser], where REF is measured on this dev M1 separately in Chrome, Safari and Firefox during the build phase.
8. Release the context with WEBGL_lose_context.loseContext() before the dynamic import of the game.
This has not been run, so no raw numbers exist yet.

findings.question: Q4 decision algorithm, thresholds and Apple disambiguation (design)
findings.answer:
First classify the GPU from the string (and the WebGPU vendor on Safari), then use the benchmark score. Placeholder thresholds: score < 55 → Low, ≥ 175 → Max.
- Apple base M1–M4 by name in Chrome → Medium.
- M-series Pro/Max/Ultra → Max.
- NVIDIA RTX xx60 and up from the 30 series onward, RTX 2070+, AMD RX 6700–6999, 7700+, 9060+ → Max.
- Old integrated GPUs (Intel UHD/Iris/Iris Xe, 'Radeon(TM) Graphics', Vega APUs) → Low, promoted to Medium only if score ≥ 120, because a short burst benchmark overestimates shared-memory iGPUs.
- Newer iGPUs (Arc iGPU, 680M–890M) and entry dGPUs → capped at Medium.
- Masked or unknown ('Apple GPU', 'Apple M1, or similar', Firefox buckets) → decided by score. In Safari, a WebGPU vendor other than 'apple' means an Intel Mac and is treated as an iGPU or mid dGPU.
- Software renderer, failed major-performance-caveat check, or phone/touch-only → Low.
- deviceMemory ≤2 → Low; ≤4 → at most Medium. hardwareConcurrency <4 → Low.
Resolution never changes the tier. It sets renderScale = clamp(sqrt(TARGET_MP[tier]/backingMP), 0.4, 1). With the placeholder medium target of 2.3 MP, this M1 at 5.18 MP gets ≈0.67 (pixel ratio 1.33), and at 'More Space' (7.06 MP) ≈0.57. findings.question: Q5 rAF cadence: 120 Hz ProMotion, Safari, Energy Saver, background tabs
findings.answer:
MDN says:
- rAF frequency 'will generally match the display refresh rate'.
- rAF is paused in background tabs and hidden iframes.
- The timestamp is the end time of the previous frame's rendering, identical for all callbacks in the same frame, with 'minimal precision of 1 millisecond'.
WebKit sets PreferPageRenderingUpdatesNear60FPSEnabled to true by default (except visionOS), so Safari runs at about 60 fps even on 120 Hz ProMotion. Chrome Energy Saver lowers the refresh rate; its blog says animations that assume 16.67 ms per frame 'run twice as slow'. So measure the vsync interval from the median of recent rAF deltas and re-estimate it periodically. Never hardcode 60 or 120. 'Uncapped' means the rAF rate. Chrome running at 120 Hz on ProMotion is not specifically verified this session.

findings.question: Q5 correct frame cap (30/60/uncapped) and pitfalls
findings.answer:
Skipping a render inside a rAF callback is safe. Per the WebGL spec, the drawing buffer is only presented if a draw happened since the last composite, so the last frame stays on screen.

The cap algorithm keeps a 'due' deadline and advances it by 1000/cap on each render. Before the vsync estimate exists it uses a 2 ms tolerance; after that it uses half a vsync interval, so jitter never halves the frame rate.

Pitfalls:
- The naive check 'elapsed ≥ interval' drops frames on jitter.
- The pattern 'then = now - elapsed % interval' drifts and bursts after stalls.
- If a stall or tab return leaves the loop more than one interval late, resync with due = t + interval instead of rendering a burst of catch-up frames.
- When the refresh rate isn't a multiple of the cap (144 Hz with a 60 cap), frames alternate between 2 and 3 vsyncs and judder. Offer a 'divisor' mode, where the cap = refresh / round(refresh / requested).
- Never pace with setTimeout/setInterval.
- On visibilitychange, reset the loop state and the FPS buffer. Use a fixed-step simulation with the frame delta clamped to about 0.1 s.
The logic was hand-traced but not executed.

findings.question: Q5 FPS counter: custom vs stats.js
findings.answer: three@0.186.1 ships stats.js at examples/jsm/libs/stats.module.js (REVISION 16). Its FPS panel computes frames*1000/(time-prevTime) once at least 1000 ms have passed. Its MS panel is the CPU time between begin() and end(), not GPU time. The MB panel appears only when performance.memory exists, which is Chromium only. It has no percentiles. The custom meter keeps a Float32Array ring of deltas between rendered frames (not between rAF callbacks), taken from rAF timestamps. It reports a ~1 s rolling average, a '1% low' (average of the slowest 1% of the last ~1200 frames) and p99 frametime as FPS. Update the DOM about 4 times per second. The 1 ms timestamp precision quantizes individual frames but is fine for averages and percentiles.

findings.question: Q5 three r186 timing utilities
findings.answer: THREE.Timer is in core (src/core/Timer.js). update(timestamp) accepts the rAF time and getDelta() returns seconds. connect(document) uses the Page Visibility API: delta is 0 while hidden and the timer resets when the page becomes visible again. THREE.Clock is deprecated since r183 and logs a warning. Use Timer, fed from the capped loop, and clamp the delta.

findings.question: Boot isolation: three.js must not load before the preset is picked
findings.answer: Vite rewrites dynamic imports to __vitePreload(() => import(chunk), deps). The helper adds the preload <link> elements and calls import() only when that code runs, so the three.js chunk is not fetched until the user picks a preset. The boot entry must have no static import chain into three or into game modules. If it does, Vite emits modulepreload links for them in the HTML. That last point comes from Vite docs; I did not trace it in source.
